what: hitop — R package for HiTOP Society questionnaire instruments
title: hitop — R package for HiTOP Society questionnaire instruments
text: Scores, validity-screens, distributes HiTOP Society instruments: PID-5 (FULL 220 / SF 100 / BF 25 / BFPM 36 / IRF 218 / FFBF 100, one function per task version argument), HiTOP-SR (405), HiTOP-BR (45), HiTOP-HSUM (item data + export ; scoring pending Society feedback). Version 0.2.0, GPL-3. Maintained Jeffrey Girard.

title: hitop — R package for HiTOP Society questionnaire instruments
text: Scoring signature: (data, items, [version,] srange, prefix, missing, calc_se, append = TRUE); always returns tibble. id/scales/tibble arguments; scales computed. Reliability separate returning family reliability_{pid5,hitopsr,hitopbr}(data, items, [version,] srange, alpha, omega) → per-scale tibble. Output columns: prefix + camelCase scale name (pid_anhedonia, hsr_...); validity scales prefix + abbreviation (pid_PNA, pid_INC); standard errors add _se. Scale membership comes *_scales list-column tables (pid_scales[[version]]$itemNumbers, hitopsr_scales, hitopbr_scales); reverse-keying validity-scale membership *_items tables. Never hardcode item numbers. User messaging via cli::cli_alert_warning() + cli::cli_alert_info() actionable {.code dplyr::filter(...)} suggestions — except reports caller meant catch suppress, cli::cli_warn() conditions (D-024/D-025 carve-, see DESIGN “User communication”); validation via validate_*()/cli_assert() R/util.R. Base-R data manipulation internally; {tibble} Import (default output), {lavaan} Suggests (needed calc_omega). Instrument administration text lives R/sysdata.rda (*_instructions); prebuilt DOCX/Qualtrics/REDCap artifacts inst/extdata/.

title: Scoring the PID-5
text: Thirty scale columns can read glance. rank_scales() function condenses : row sorts columns select returns single string naming highest-scoring ones, highest first. rank 25 facet scales — first 25 columns scored tibble, last 5 domains facets roll — ask participant’s top 5. Setting prefix = "pid_" strips leading string column names, string reads scale names. top_scales column holds one comma-separated string per participant: names five highest-scoring facets, descending order. text: numeric scalar giving Cronbach's alpha (typically [0, 1], can outside range problematic data).

title: Compute Cronbach's Coefficient Alpha — calc_alpha
text: Let \(k\) number items let \(X_1,\ldots,X_k\) denote item scores. Define total score \(T = \sum_{=1}^k X_i\). Cronbach's alpha can written without matrix notation $$\alpha   \;=\; \frac{k}{k-1}\left(1 - \frac{\sum_{=1}^k   \mathrm{Var}(X_i)}{\mathrm{Var}(T)}\right).$$ words: take sum item variances divide variance total score; subtract ratio 1 multiply \(k/(k-1)\). \(\mathrm{Var}(X_i)\) \(\mathrm{Var}(T)\) computed using pairwise-complete observations. @section Coercion: column coerced via .numeric(). means: factors converted integer level codes (labels); characters parsable numbers become NA; dates/times become underlying numeric representations. Ensure columns truly numeric item responses pre-process needed.

title: Compute Cronbach's Coefficient Alpha — calc_alpha
text: Cronbach, L. J. (1951). Coefficient alpha internal structure tests. Psychometrika, 16(3), 297–334. Sijtsma, K. (2009). use, misuse, limited usefulness Cronbach's alpha. Psychometrika, 74(1), 107–120.

text: model f =~ item1 + item2 + ... + itemK std.lv = TRUE (.e., \(\mathrm{Var}(f)=1\)). \(\omega = \frac{(\sum_i \lambda_i)^2} {(\sum_i \lambda_i)^2 + \sum_i \theta_i}\), \(\lambda_i\) unstandardized loadings \(\theta_i\) unstandardized residual variances indicators. function validates inputs fails informative messages CFA converge implied residual variances invalid. Mixed-sign loadings trigger warning (often indicates reverse-keying needed). Note latent variable estimated f, please avoid naming items .

Select the # item columns by name: `m$items` holds original HiTOP-SR numbers, which are # column positions only in a data frame that is exactly the 405 items in order. m <- hitop_module("hitopsr", scales = c("Agoraphobia", "Appetite Loss")) collected <- sim_hitopsr[sprintf("hsr_%03d", m$items)] reliability_hitopsr(collected, items = names(collected), module = m, omega = FALSE) #> # A tibble: 2 × 4 #>   Scale         camelCase    nItems    alpha #>   <chr>         <chr>         <int>    <dbl> #> 1 Agoraphobia   agoraphobia       5 -0.108   #> 2 Appetite Loss appetiteLoss      3  0.00603  # The same for data entered off a shuffled form: the columns are in the # order the form printed its items, recorded on the module's `item_order` # attribute (here set by hand; a descriptor written with `randomize = TRUE` # carries it). attr(m, "item_order") <- c(144L, 202L, 66L, 389L, 260L, 109L, 291L, 118L) printed <- collected[match(attr(m, "item_order"), m$items)] reliability_hitopsr(printed, items = seq_along(printed), module = m,                     layout = "printed", omega = FALSE) #> # A tibble: 2 × 4 #>   Scale         camelCase    nItems    alpha #>   <chr>         <chr>         <int>    <dbl> #> 1 Agoraphobia   agoraphobia       5 -0.108   #> 2 Appetite Loss appetiteLoss      3  0.00603

their columns follow the 76 scale columns score_hitopsr(sim_hitopsr, items = 1:405, include_subscales = TRUE,               append = FALSE) #> # A tibble: 100 × 93 #>    hsr_agoraphobia hsr_antisocialBehavior hsr_appearanceFocus hsr_appetiteLoss #>              <dbl>                  <dbl>               <dbl>            <dbl> #>  1             2.8                   2.75                 2.8             2.67 #>  2             2.6                   2.75                 2.8             3    #>  3             2.4                   2.75                 2.4             2.67 #>  4             2.4                   2.38                 3.4             2    #>  5             2.6                   2.5                  1.8             2    #>  6             2.4                   3.12                 2.2             2.67 #>  7             2.6                   2.38                 2.4             2.33 #>  8             3                     2.38                 3.2             2.67 #>  9             2.4                   2.38                 2.2             1.67 #> 10             2.4                   2                    3               2.33 #> # ℹ 90 more rows #> # ℹ 89 more variables: hsr_bingeEating <dbl>, hsr_bodilyDistress <dbl>, #> #   hsr_bodyDissatisfaction <dbl>, hsr_callousness <dbl>, hsr_checking <dbl>, #> #   hsr_cleaning <dbl>, hsr_cognitiveProblems <dbl>, #> #   hsr_conversionSymptoms <dbl>, hsr_counting <dbl>, #> #   hsr_dietaryRestraint <dbl>, hsr_difficultiesReachingOrgasm <dbl>, #> #   hsr_diseaseConviction <dbl>, hsr_dishonesty <dbl>, …  # Score data collected with a two-scale module. Select the item columns # by name: `m$items` holds original HiTOP-SR numbers, which are column # positions only in a data frame that is exactly the 405 items in order. m <- hitop_module("hitopsr", scales = c("Agoraphobia", "Appetite Loss")) collected <- sim_hitopsr[sprintf("hsr_%03d", m$items)] score_hitopsr(collected, items = names(collected), module = m, append = FALSE) #> # A tibble: 100 × 2 #>    hsr_agoraphobia hsr_appetiteLoss #>              <dbl>            <dbl> #>  1             2.8             2.67 #>  2             2.6             3    #>  3             2.4             2.67 #>  4             2.4             2    #>  5             2.6             2    #>  6             2.4             2.67 #>  7             2.6             2.33 #>  8             3               2.67 #>  9             2.4             1.67 #> 10             2.4             2.33 #> # ℹ 90 more rows  # Score data entered off a shuffled form: the columns are in the order the # form printed its items, recorded on the module's `item_order` attribute # (here set by hand; a descriptor written with `randomize = TRUE` carries it). attr(m, "item_order") <- c(144L, 202L, 66L, 389L, 260L, 109L, 291L, 118L) printed <- collected[match(attr(m, "item_order"), m$items)] score_hitopsr(printed, items = seq_along(printed), module = m,               layout = "printed", append = FALSE) #> # A tibble: 100 × 2 #>    hsr_agoraphobia hsr_appetiteLoss #>              <dbl>            <dbl> #>  1             2.8             2.67 #>  2             2.6             3    #>  3             2.4             2.67 #>  4             2.4             2    #>  5             2.6             2    #>  6             2.4             2.67 #>  7             2.6             2.33 #>  8             3               2.67 #>  9             2.4             1.67 #> 10             2.4             2.33 #> # ℹ 90 more rows
